title: Cup Noodle launching “isekai” crossover line featuring flavors from outside instant ramen world
description: An isekai trip for your taste buds, no truck accident required. Isekai translates to “alternate world,” but within the Japanese pop culture sphere it’s also the name of a genre of anime, novels, and other media in which someone gets transported from our mundane plane of existence to a realm with new adventures waiting for […]
content:
An isekai trip for your taste buds, no truck accident required.

Isekai translates to “alternate world,” but within the Japanese pop culture sphere it’s also the name of a genre of anime, novels, and other media in which someone gets transported from our mundane plane of existence to a realm with new adventures waiting for them. A salaryman might be whisked away to a second life as a spacefaring explorer, or a schoolgirl might awaken to find herself reborn in a kingdom where she’s now part of a web of romantic courtly intrigue.

But now it’s Cup Noodles’ turn to get isekai-ed, as Nissin has announced three new flavors that combine their instant noodles with other beloved food brands from outside the cup ramen world.

First up for the Cup Noodle Isekai Gattai series (gattai meaning “combination”) is a collaboration between the standard Cup Noodle flavor and Gindaco, one of Japan’s most popular takoyaki (octopus ball) chains.

The familiar Cup Noodle broth gets enhancements of extra dashi (bonito stock), and the customary takoyaki ingredients of powdered seaweed, pickled ginger, plus flavors evocative of the sweet sauce that’s squirted on the dumplings. Inside the cup, Cup Noodle’s iconic “mystery meat” is joined by the similarly mysterious-sounding “octopus-style balls.” There’s also an extra packet of oil on the side to add after the noodles cook as a salute to the oil that Gindako adds to its takoyaki.

Next up is a meeting of the worlds of Curry Cup noodle and Karamucho, Japan’s spiciest mass-market crisp potato stick snacks.

The already piquant curry broth gets its heat turned up a notch with the addition of chilies, plus garlic too. Floating in that spicy/savory mix are pieces of chili-spiced potato, mystery meat, and carrots.

And finally, Seafood Cup Noodle joins forces with Gohan Desu Yo, a brand of simmered seaweed. Gohan Desu Yo is usually eaten by adding a small spoonful to a bowl of white rice, but for this team-up you get a packet of simmered seaweed paste to squeeze into the broth after cooking. That broth is based on the Seafood Cup Noodle, but with extra seaweed, and the oceanic theme continues with pieces of squid and imitation crab, plus cabbage, egg, and green onion.

All three varieties are priced at 259 yen (US$1.65) scheduled to go on sale November 9.

Source: Nissin via Golden Times

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new Christmas goods for 2026, with exclusive holiday surprises
description: Festive cheer is here, with mugs, tumblers, candles and keychains you won’t find at any other time of year.  It’s that time of year again, when we look at the calendar and realise there’s now less than eight weeks until Christmas. That means it’s time for Starbucks to start bringing us some holiday cheer, and […]
content:
Festive cheer is here, with mugs, tumblers, candles and keychains you won’t find at any other time of year. 

It’s that time of year again, when we look at the calendar and realise there’s now less than eight weeks until Christmas. That means it’s time for Starbucks to start bringing us some holiday cheer, and this year it’s doing that with a massive collection of festive goods based around the theme of “Colours of Holiday“.

Red, green, white and gold are the main colours in the collection, with Bearistas and ribbons adding an extra touch of cuteness and glamour to the festivities. There are a lot of wonderful surprises in store, including a trio of exclusive candles, so let’s take a closer look at everything in the range, which Starbucks says will “brighten your heart for the holiday season”.

▼ Holiday 2026 Gift Box Stainless Steel Bottle, Glitter Red, 473 millilitres (16 ounces), 5,550 yen (US$34.86)

This glittery bottle will add a touch of festive flair to your drinking experience during the holidays, but it can also be used all year long.

▼ Easy to cheer, easy to clean.

▼ Holiday 2026 Gift Box with Canister and Ribbon (3,500 yen)

▼ This canister takes the look of a Starbucks cup…

▼ …and gives it a ceramic makeover, transforming it into the perfect vessel for storing your coffee beans.

▼ Beans not included.

▼ Holiday 2026 Gift Box Double-Walled Heat-Resistant Glass with Ribbon (355 millilitres, 3,800 yen)

▼ This glass might look small in the image above, but seeing it in a human hand conveys its true size.

Though the glass itself is massive, the portion that holds the liquid has a 355-millilitre capacity. The rest of the glass is occupied by a beautiful red ribbon, and glittery gold pieces that swirl around every time you take a sip.

 

▼ Holiday 2026 Gift Boxed Stacking Mug Set (237 millilitres, 4,800 yen)

These mugs stack beautifully within each other, creating a cheerful festive duo that can easily be used throughout the year.

▼ Holiday 2026 Gift Boxed Cold Cup Tumbler Figure (473 millilitres, 4,250 yen)

This is another massive vessel that holds a lot of liquid, but your eye will be quickly distracted by the beautiful festive scene at the top of the tumbler.

A bright red bow and a Bearista keep you company as you sip, and they’ll stay firmly in place even when the tumbler is tilted.

▼ Holiday 2026 Gift Box Glass Tumbler Bearista, 473 millilitres (4,600 yen)

This is one of the cutest items in the whole collection, as the colour of the bear changes depending on the drink inside it. Fill it with milk and you’ll have yourself a white bear, while a black coffee will turn it dark and a latte will give it a delicious light brown hue.

▼ Not only is the bear cute, it’s also easy to clean.

▼ Rounding out the drinkware items is the Holiday 2026 Reusable Cup Tree, 473 millilitres (500 yen)…

▼ …and the Holiday 2026 Reusable Cup Tree 473 millilitres + Holiday 2026 Reusable Cup Dedicated Drink Hole Cap Bearista Tree (1,150 yen)

▼ Moving on to the notebooks, we have the Starbucks Holiday 2026 Campus Ring Notebook Tree (650 yen)…

▼ …and the Journal Book (2,050 yen).

The festive season is a time for gifting, and to help with that are a series of food and drink tickets and beverage cards.

▼ Holiday 2026 Food & Beverage Card – includes food & drink tickets (1,100yen)

▼ Holiday 2026 Beverage Card Tree, with drink ticket (900 yen)

▼ This card becomes your own mini tabletop Christmas tree.

▼ Starbucks Holiday 2026 Mini Cup Gift Red Cup, with drink ticket (1,150 yen)

This is a gift you’ll want to keep for yourself, as the mini cup looks like a tiny Starbucks cup, with a bright festive design.

▼ It also comes with a beautiful mint-green bag…

▼ …and can be used to store small items like paper clips.

▼ Holiday 2026 Bearista Message Gift, with drink ticket (1,650 yen)

▼ A beary cute way to treat someone to a beverage.

 

 

▼ Holiday 2026 Craft Paper Shopper S (2,400 yen)

▼ This nifty bag is a beautiful way to carry, or gift, one or more of the bottles in the collection.

▼ Holiday 2026 Cup-Shaped Pouch with Keychain & Mirror (2,600 yen)

▼ Holiday 2026 Bearista (5,500 yen)

▼ Holiday 2026 Gift Boxed Plush Ornament Set (3,500 yen)

▼ This set lets you decorate your tree with a couple of Starbucks ornaments…

▼ … that are a lot bigger than they seem.

▼ Bearista Keychain Set in Holiday 2026 Gift Box (4,500 yen)

This cute item looks set to be a sell-out hit, as the Bearista comes with a change of clothes and a couple of cute snowy companions, creating a very unique type of keychain.

 

Finally, we have a trio of candles, which can only be purchased at the online store.

▼ Starbucks Moment Refresh Inspired by Yuzu Citrus & Tea (3,800 yen)

▼ Starbucks Moment Joy Inspired by Joyful Medley (3,800 yen)

▼ Starbucks Moment Relax Inspired by Coffee & Spice (3,800 yen)

There’s a lot of joy to be found in the holiday collection, but as always, it will only be around for a limited time while stocks last. This year, online sales will commence at 8:00 p.m. on 30 October, while in-store sales will start on 2 November. Be sure to act quick to grab your favourites!

Source, images: Press release

title: Japan getting a brand-new batch of Pokémon manhole covers in eastern prefecture this fall
description: Five new reasons for Pokémon fans to head north from Tokyo. Fall is a fantastic time to take a trip to Gunma Prefecture. Located about two hours north of Tokyo, Gunma gets some beautiful autumn foliage and it also boasts some of east Japan’s finest hot springs, making for a great combo of crisp afternoon […]
content:
Five new reasons for Pokémon fans to head north from Tokyo.

Fall is a fantastic time to take a trip to Gunma Prefecture. Located about two hours north of Tokyo, Gunma gets some beautiful autumn foliage and it also boasts some of east Japan’s finest hot springs, making for a great combo of crisp afternoon walks followed by a rejuvenatingly warm soak.

As of this fall, there’s one more reason to head to Gunma. Well, five actually, as the prefecture is getting five new Pokémon manhole covers!

The Pokéfuta/Poké Lids project is a series of artistic one-of-a-kind manhole covers highlighting local communities, helping to draw visitors to lesser-known but still charming parts of Japan. The covers all feature Pocket Monster species and local scenery or representative products such as produce or handicrafts. For example, the Gunma town of Shimonita takes great pride in the quality of the green onions that its farmers grow, so naturally its Pokéfuta, installed in front of the Coconita building next to Shimonita Station, features Farfetch’d, Galarian Farfetch’d, and Sirfetch’d.

Boltund naturally feels at home playing in front of Yamba Dam, a towering hydroelectric facility in the town of Naganohara. Joining the Electric-type on this cover, which will be at the Yamba Furusato-kan michi no eki (“road station” local products shop) are Meltan and Seaking, creating further tie-ins with the water/engineering theme.

Zigzagoon, in both standard and Galarian forms, appears on the Pokéfuta for the Tsutsujigaoka Fureai Center, located inside Tsutsujigaoka Park in the town of Tatebayashi. This one might actually be best to wait until spring to visit, as tsutsuji is the Japanese word for azalea, and the park contains some 10,000 bushes on which the seasonal flowers bloom.

Dunsparce and Shiftry can be seen hanging out on their manhole cover at the entrance to the hiking trail that leads to Fukiware Falls in the town of Numata, placed next to the parking area that hikers can use. Shiftry is here because his design is based on the tengu (crow spirits) of Japanese folklore, who are often depicted using giant leaves or fans to create strong gusts of wind. Tengu are prominently featured in the folklore surrounding Numata’s Miroku Temple on Mt. Kasho, which claims to have the largest tengu mask in all of Japan.

And finally, as you board or exit the Shibukawa Ikaho Ropeway at Hototogisu Station in the town of Shibukawa, you’ll be able to say hi to Zapdos, who, being a Flying-type Pokémon, can enjoy expansive views and mountain scenery without having to ride one of the ropeway’s gondolas.

▼ The Pokéfuta locations within Gunma Prefecture

All five new Pokémon manhole covers are scheduled to be installed by the end of November.

Source: Gunma Prefecture, Jiji

title: One simple unexpected recipe swap will make your Japanese-style omelets extra fluffy and juicy
description: And one more cooking hack will make your dashimaki tamago fluffier still. In terms of ingredients, dashimaki tamago is an incredibly simple dish. A type of Japanese omelet, you can make it with just three ingredients: eggs, water, and dashi (a stock made from fish and kelp that’s found in all sorts of Japanese dishes). […]
content:
And one more cooking hack will make your dashimaki tamago fluffier still.

In terms of ingredients, dashimaki tamago is an incredibly simple dish. A type of Japanese omelet, you can make it with just three ingredients: eggs, water, and dashi (a stock made from fish and kelp that’s found in all sorts of Japanese dishes). The cooking process is also pretty straightforward, or maybe paradoxically straightforward, since dashimaki tamago is basically an omelet that you wrap (maku) back over itself multiple times, using a rectangular frying pan if you want the traditional squared-off shape.

But just because dashimaki tamago is simple doesn’t mean it’s easy to make. The process can be surprisingly delicate, and while anyone with minimal cooking skills will be able to make dashimaki tamago that’s edible, it takes a deft hand to make dashimaki tamago with a wonderfully fluffy texture throughout its layers. So when we heard rumors of an unexpected ingredient substitution that’s supposed to make dashimaki tamago extra fluffy, we were all attentive ears and growling stomachs.

First, let’s run through the basics of how to make dashimaki tamago. You’ll need:
● 3 eggs
● 1 tablespoon of dashi (we used the type called shirodashi)
● 3 tablespoons of water

Mix them all up in a bowl, and also heat up an oiled frying pan on medium heat. Pour 1/3 of the mixture into the pan, give it a little mix with cooking chopsticks, and once it’s half-cooked, roll it to the front half of the pan. Reoil the now vacant part of the pan, add half of the ingredient mixture, and repeat the cooking and rolling process, then do it all again for the remainder of the mixture.

So what’s the cooking hack substitution we’re trying today? Using sparkling/carbonated water instead of regular water.

We heard about this idea through Asahi TV’s news/talk program Tantei! Knight Scoop, and then our reporter Natsuki Gojo headed into the SoraKitchen to test it out. Aside from the water swap, there’s only one other change to make, which is that when using the sparkling water, you mix the egg and dashi together first, and then add in the sparkling water right before cooking.

OK, let’s see if this sparkling water swap really is such a bright idea!

▼ Regular water (left) and sparkling water (right)

Starting with how the mixture of the three ingredients looked prior to cooking, as you can see in the above photo there’s a noticeable amount of fizz introduced by the sparkling water…at least initially. After stirring, though, the bubbles died down, and the regular and sparkling mixtures were equally calm.

Once Natsuki poured them into the pan, though, the bubbles came back to the sparkling mix in a big way.

Once both dashimaki tamago were done cooking, we laid them out side by side on a plate, and sure enough, the sparkling version had cooked up bigger and plumper, despite both versions having the exact same volume of ingredients.

Next we sliced off a piece from each to examine their cross-sections, and were happy to see that the sparkling water substitution had produced exactly the sort of results we’d been hoping for!

The regular-water version had congealed towards the bottom of the roll, but the sparkling dashimaki tamago had maintained a nice network of little air pockets while cooking, and those had made it fluffier. It wasn’t just the texture that had been enhanced, either. The sparkling dashimaki tamago was juicier too.

Emboldened by this success, Natsuki decided to whip up one more batch of dashimaki tamago to test out another rumor she’d heard for further fluffiness. This time, instead of using three tablespoons of sparkling water, she used 175 milliliters (5.9 ounces), or roughly 10 tablespoons.

Unsurprisingly, this resulted in even more bubbles at the pre-mix and cooking stages, and Natsuki found herself worried that the mixture might be too watery to cook up properly.

But those fears turned out to be unnecessary, and this high-volume sparkling water version was the fluffiest and juiciest of all three she cooked.

▼ Sparkling water dashimaki tamago (left) and high-volume sparkling water dashimaki tamago (right)

Natsuki herself is quick to point out that she doesn’t have a ton of experience cooking her own dashimaki tamago, so we’re not saying that using sparkling water is a must for good results. At the same time, her relative inexperience proves that you don’t have to be an expert to benefit from this simple ingredient swap, so if you’re looking to make your Japanese-style omelets as fluffy as you can, this is definitely worth giving a shot.

Reference: Asahi TV, Ninben

title: This curry restaurant might have the worst location in Tokyo…or maybe the best
description: Alk Road finds a way to turn a negative into a positive. There are a lot of curry restaurants to choose from in Tokyo, but Spice Curry Alk Road stands out from many of its rice-and-roux rivals by virtue of its outstanding customer reviews. Diners are so satisfied that they’ve made Alk Road one of […]
content:
Alk Road finds a way to turn a negative into a positive.

There are a lot of curry restaurants to choose from in Tokyo, but Spice Curry Alk Road stands out from many of its rice-and-roux rivals by virtue of its outstanding customer reviews. Diners are so satisfied that they’ve made Alk Road one of the top 100 curry restaurants in Tokyo based on average review scores on Tabelog, Japan’s most popular user-submitted restaurant site.

Alk Road is just a one-minute walk from Iidabashi Station, so you could say that it has a great location…but as we found out on our visit, you could also make an argument that it has the worst location for a curry restaurant in Tokyo. If you head to the restaurant’s address, you’ll find yourself in front of this building.

And yes, you will see the word “curry,” written in Japanese as カレー, on the signage.

But the writing in front of “curry,” 上等? They’re the characters for “Joto,” as in “Joto Curry,” a curry restaurant chain that is not the independent Alk Road.

So if you were to amble up here, you might think that Alk Road has gone out of business and been replaced by a Joto branch. A restaurant closing down and then a different one with the same specialty moving into the same spot isn’t all that unusual in Japan, since it lowers the renovation costs that you might have with, say, converting a yakiniku restaurant into a conveyor belt sushi joint.

However, if you look down at the entrance to Joto Curry, you’ll see that Alk Road’s name is written next to the door…

…and both Joto Curry’s and Alk Road’s names are written on the noren (cloth banner) hung above the entrance.

Things get even more confusing when you step inside, since the first floor is clearly a Joto Curry branch. If you want to find Alk Road, what you have to do is turn to your right…

…and follow the arrows pointing you up the stairs to the second floor…

…and then, finally, you’ll have arrived at Alk Road!

View this post on Instagram

Yes, Alk Road has the confusing misfortune of being a curry restaurant that you can only access by first passing part-way through a different curry restaurant, and one that’s part of a famous chain to boot.

This might seem like a recipe for constant animosity between the upstairs/downstairs neighbors, but it turns out that Joto Curry and Alk Road aren’t exactly direct competitors. Whereas Joto’s specialty is Japanese-style curry, Alk Road’s focus is on Indian-style curry, which the second-floor restaurant’s chef makes from scratch every day.

While they’re both variations on the same basic concept (curry and rice), they use different kinds of roux, and different kinds of rice too – long-grain Indian rice for Alkroad’s curry, and short-grain Japanese rice for Joto Curry’s. So among diners in Japan, these two restaurants’ offerings are scratching different culinary itches, and even if you are in a perfectly 50-50 mood as to which type of curry they were craving, Alk Road actually offers a way to enjoy both in the same meal.

One of Alk Road’s menu items is the Special Combination, a plate of curry rice in which one half is Joto’s roux and a pork cutlet, and the other is your choice of one of Alk Road’s house-specialty spice curries.

▼ Our 1,400-yen (US$8.80) Special Combination of Johto katsu curry and Alk Road chicken spice curry

You also choose between Indian and Japanese rice for the Special Combination. We asked for the Indian rice, which made for a unique mixture of flavors and textures when paired with the Japanese roux. Both curries were excellent on their own, with Alk Road’s giving us a complex mixture of spices and seasonings and Joto’s being a more straightforward spiciness with a hint of sweetness in its flavor profile, and at the center of the plate where it flowed into one another we got yet another intriguingly fresh flavor.

Should you want even more variety, Alk Road’s counter has an array of spices that you can shake onto your curry at your discretion, such as Cayenne pepper, roasted cumin, garam masala, and ajwain chili powder.

This one-of-a-kind collaborative curry combination is something that’s only possible by nature of having two different curry restaurants operating so close to one another, and through it Alk Road has cleverly turned a negative aspect of its location into a positive. So while the search for Alk Road might be a little confusing, it’s well worth going to the trouble to find, just like with a certain soft serve ice cream specialist elsewhere in Tokyo.

Restaurant information
Spice Curry Alk Road / Spice Curry アルクロード
Address: Tokyo-to, Chiyoda-ku, Iidabashi 4-8-11 2nd floor
住所　東京都千代田区飯田橋4丁目8−11 2F
Open 11 a.m.-3 p.m., 5:30 p.m.-10:30 p.m. (weekdays), 11 a.m.-3 p.m., 530 p.m.-8 p.m. (weekends, holidays)

title: Baum vending machine in a Yokohama station lets us eat cake served on a luxury cruise ship
description: Our favorite kind wasn’t even the one we expected, but they were all the baum-dot-com. It takes a lot to surprise us when it comes to Japanese vending machines, considering we’ve seen everything from Sriracha to sushi meals being sold in them. While the latter might sound a bit dubious, we’ve had relatively good results […]
content:
Our favorite kind wasn’t even the one we expected, but they were all the baum-dot-com.

It takes a lot to surprise us when it comes to Japanese vending machines, considering we’ve seen everything from Sriracha to sushi meals being sold in them. While the latter might sound a bit dubious, we’ve had relatively good results with the weird and wacky, and we’re always keeping our eyes peeled for new discoveries.

The latest unusual vending machine we spotted was right outside of the ticket gates at Bashamichi Station on Yokohama’s Minatomirai Line. It was actually attracting a lot of curious glances from passersby, most likely because it was filled with Baumkuchen, the German spit cake that’s incredibly popular in Japan and usually goes by just “baum.”

▼ Cake from a vending machine somehow feels a lot safer than sushi.

A closer look at the sign revealed that this particular baum was produced by Cocotomo Farm, which makes a 100-percent gluten-free cake using homemade rice flour from Aichi Prefecture. According to the sign, its brown rice-based hard baum is even given as a welcome gift on the luxury Asuka III cruise ship–Japan’s largest passenger ship–and was being sold in this machine at a discounted price to reduce food waste.

Apparently there’s an Asuka III Meets 47 Prefectures Project, and this brand was selected as a representative for the Aichi Prefecture Room. As for why it’s being sold at this particular nondescript station in Yokohama, well, that part’s still a mystery–but perhaps it’s because there are several international cruise ship terminals in the area.

There were plenty of baum options in the vending machine, but none of the selections were for the brown rice-based hard baum variety alone. Therefore, we opted for a combo pack with a slice of that one along with a slice of the white rice-based soft baum for 650 yen (US$4.14), as well as a pack of hard baum edges for 500 yen.

▼ The machine takes cash or a variety of payment apps.

All of the baum in this machine are frozen to preserve their freshness, so our prizes were quite chilly when they first came out. Luckily, the weather was relatively warm on this particular day, and the slices of cake had thawed out well by the time we got home. Here they were in their simple, unpretentious packaging.

We were journalistically obligated to then immediately sample the slices of the soft and hard varieties, which were individually packaged.

▼ Soft baum (top) and hard baum (bottom)

The soft baum was true to its name and had a refined, moist texture. We would have never known that it was gluten-free if the packaging didn’t alert us. Meanwhile, the hard baum had the exact opposite kind of feel. It was densely packed and required some force to bite down on, being chewy at the same time. It also carried the distinctive almost nut-like flavor of brown rice. We had always assumed that all baum tasted more or less the same, but this sampling threw that notion far out the window.

Next, we broke out the hard baum edges. There were six individual pieces of slightly varying sizes packed into one bag.

The hard baum edges were, if anything, even more densely packed with flavor and texture than the soft baum and regular hard baum alike. Sure, they were rough-looking on the outside, but they hid an intense surprise on the inside.

In fact, they ended up being our favorite of the whole bunch. The value of six pieces for that price was also hard to beat.

We have no idea how long the Cocotomo Farm vending machine is going to be stationed at Bashamichi Station–but we suppose that whenever it goes away, we’ll just have to get our baum fix from the ample varieties sold at at Muji instead.

title: Visiting the “world’s most precarious temple” in China, where getting there is half the battle
description: Xuankong Si is surprisingly both extremely out of the way and extremely crowded. Our writer Seiji recently visited China, where he got a haircut on the side of the road and did some sightseeing. One of these sights was none other than Xuankong Si, or “The Hanging Temple” in English. Its name says it all […]
content:
Xuankong Si is surprisingly both extremely out of the way and extremely crowded.

Our writer Seiji recently visited China, where he got a haircut on the side of the road and did some sightseeing. One of these sights was none other than Xuankong Si, or “The Hanging Temple” in English. Its name says it all really, in that it’s a temple clinging for dear life to the side of a sheer cliff.

This temple is located in the Jinxia Gorge at the foot of Mt. Heng, known as one of China’s five great mountains. Of course, getting to a mystical temple like this was never meant to be easy and required Seiji to take a high-speed train from Beijing to Datong South Station, then drive from there into the mountains for about an hour.

▼ Seiji with his new haircut modeled after World Cup sensation Erling Haaland

It was quite a haul, but Seiji was completely enamored with the Chinese countryside. The winding mountain roads reminded him perfectly of the area where Goku first met Bulma in Dragon Ball. There was a pulse of exotic adventure everywhere he looked.

Little did he know, however, that his true battle still lay ahead. The visitor center leading into the temple area was far less mystical than other parts of his journey.

The ticket counter opens at 7:30 a.m., and Seiji arrived at 8:40. However, he was told that the tickets had already sold out. As luck would have it, tickets are sold in two batches, with 600 in the morning and another 600 in the afternoon. This meant he’d have to wait until noon to try again.

By 10 a.m.,  a significant lineup was already forming, and Seiji watched with amazement as it just got bigger…

…and bigger…

…and bigger…

…and bigger with time. By noon, it looked exactly like the line to get into Comiket.

It’s actually possible to book tickets in advance, but only for Chinese residents. This meant Seiji had no choice but to wait in line, but as he listened to two old ladies shouting at each other, he wondered why all these other people didn’t just make reservations.

Luckily, this time he could get tickets. Two types are sold: a general admission to the area for 15 yuan (US$2.25) and access to the temple itself for 100 yuan ($15). Considering how much effort it took to get this far, there was no way he was going to skip entering The Hanging Temple.

From this point, a bus ride was required, but it only took eight minutes and cost 20 yuan. But after all that traveling and waiting, he was happy to see that it was all worth it for this spectacular scenery.

This temple was mentioned on Time Magazine’s Top 10 Precarious Buildings, and since it was the only temple on the list, Seiji figures it’s safe to call it the world’s most precarious temple.

In this case, the word “precarious” doesn’t suggest poor construction or actual hazards, but a certain tilt that gives the feeling of precariousness.

This place certainly had that feeling in spades. As he walked along narrow paths jutting out from sheer cliffs that seemed to tower over him, the ground spread out far, far below him.

Seiji was never especially afraid of heights, but here he occasionally felt a little woozy and had to brace himself against the wall.

This structure was around 1,500 years old, and as is often the case with older buildings, everything feels a little smaller than usual. The railings everywhere were only about waist-height, adding to a sense that he was walking through the air.

▼ No problem there.

It truly felt like a temple in the sky, giving our writer a sensation he often felt during dreams where he was flying but then suddenly forgot how to fly and plummeted back to Earth. 

It was a one-of-a-kind experience and well-steeped in Chinese culture.

Seiji felt a sense of awe beyond most other places he’s been in his life, and would highly recommend a visit to anyone.

His only advice is to purchase the ticket to enter the temple, because it’d be a waste to travel all that way and not climb up to it. Also, make sure you arrive early because the lineup for tickets is no joke, and it’d be an even bigger waste to travel all that way and not even be able to get near Xuankong Si.

Temple information
The Hanging Temple / 懸空寺
Hanging Temple, Jinlong Gorge, Mount Heng, Hunyuan County, Datong, Shanxi Province, China

Ticket Sales Begin: 7:30 a.m. and Noon
Holidays: None

title: Beloved, 100-year-old Tokyo public bathhouse Sengenyu is about to get a second life this December
description: Various entities take a dip together to save a community institution and preserve public bath culture for the next generation to enjoy. Public bathhouses, known as sento in Japanese, have long served as important community gathering hubs where different generations can interact with one another. Unfortunately, not all public baths are able to stay afloat […]
content:
Various entities take a dip together to save a community institution and preserve public bath culture for the next generation to enjoy.

Public bathhouses, known as sento in Japanese, have long served as important community gathering hubs where different generations can interact with one another. Unfortunately, not all public baths are able to stay afloat in this age of rising costs and other factors. Case in point: from 2015 to 2025, the number of public bathhouses operating in Tokyo dropped from 628 to 417 locations.

Thankfully, one public bath in Tokyo’s Nerima Ward called Sengenyu is not going to join those statistics anytime soon. First opened in 1927, the third-generation previous owner was on the verge of closing the beloved community staple due to their family’s increasing age and the deteriorating facilities. However, thanks to the Tokyo Public Bathhouse Succession Matching Program offered jointly by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government and the Tokyo Public Bathhouses Association, a new owner in company Ofuro Works was found. Now, instead of being demolished, Sengenyu is currently being renovated and will reopen to the public in early December.

▼ The current exterior of Sengenyu

The project includes large-scale remodeling of Sengenyu’s entrance, lobby, changing rooms, and saunas to update certain facilities.

▼ Rendition of the completed exterior, designed to blend in with the surrounding area

The lobby is particular is intended to become a spacious, relaxing entryway where patrons can soak in the warmth of the natural wood theme inside.

In addition, a new electric heater from Japanese bath company Metos will be installed within the saunas. Patrons can continue to throw water on the rocks themselves in order to increase the steam to their desired level.

These new updates don’t mean that Sengenyu will lose all of its original charm, though, as features such as the retro-style bathroom with its colorful tile art and the Shigaraki ware tanuki statue outside will be preserved in its redesign.

In a delightful community collaboration, Ofuro Works is also partnering with students at the local Nihon University College of Art to design an updated logo and mascot character based on the tanuki statue. It’s a true full-circle moment, as students from this school as well as other local universities have long been going to Sengenyu and can now leave their own personal mark on the space for many more years to come.

Finally, widespread public fundraising efforts are set to begin on November 1 through Japan’s largest crowdfunding site, Campfire. The project aims to raise 1 million yen (US$6,375) to help offset the costs of remodeling and updating the bath facilities. Financial backers will receive a towel, t-shirt, and a sneak-peek of Sengenyu behind the scenes before it reopens for business.

▼ The art students’ new logo combines the steam of a bathhouse with the puff of smoke that occurs when a tanuki transforms in Japanese folklore.

Despite the decrease in the total number of Tokyo public bathhouses, we can only hope that the statistics showing that the number of users is actually going up will allow Sengenyu and other bath facilities in the Greater Tokyo Area to flourish for 100 more years and beyond.

Bath information
Sengenyu / 浅間湯
Address: Tokyo-to, Nerima-ku, Sakae-cho 38-3
東京都練馬区栄町 38-3
Reopens in early December
Open (new hours): 3 p.m.-11 p.m.
Closed (new day): Mondays
